An energetic group from Córdoba that, without grand ambitions, aims to give its best and tackle whatever comes our way.
summary: Cultivito is a decision-support tool for agricultural matters. Using NASA data, it allows for satellite monitoring of a specific plot of land, providing a ranking of recommended crops and a recommended rotation sequence (which can be adjusted based on up to previous rotations). Developed based on real pain points faced by small-scale farmers, the tool aims to provide them with an accessible and useful resource.
details:
Cultivito delivers intelligent crop-rotation suggests to support agricultural decision-making, through an integrated process of geospatial, satellite, and historical analysis.

Field location and boundaries: The user marks the exact plot or agricultural area on an interactive map, or enters precise latitude and longitude coordinates.

Satellite monitoring and climate data: The platform performs field-specific satellite tracking using NASA climate and hydrological data (from sources such as NASA SMAP, GPM, OpenET, and HLS).

Agronomic history assessment: Users can record up to 3 previous crops (the immediate predecessor, two cycles ago, and three cycles ago). This history is analyzed to:

  • Assess residual nitrogen (N) fixation in the soil.
  • Promote biological alternation between species.
  • Prevent problems caused by monoculture.

Recommendation generation: After processing the field data and environmental conditions, the tool calculates and delivers two main results:

  • A ranking of crops with the best options for the plot.
  • A recommended rotation sequence adapted to the soil’s previous dynamics.

Key benefits

Cultivito offers the following key benefits for agricultural management:

  • Monoculture prevention: Lets users record up to 3 previous harvests to avoid the degradation problems caused by monoculture.
  • Soil nutrient assessment: Measures the residual nitrogen (N) fixation left by previous plantings.
  • Biological alternation: Helps plan a proper alternation of plant species in the field.
  • Precise satellite and environmental monitoring: Integrates NASA satellite and climate data (such as NASA SMAP, GPM, OpenET, and HLS) for continuous monitoring of the land.
  • Strategic recommendations: Delivers a ranking of optimal crops and suggests a recommended rotation sequence adapted to the specific conditions of the plot.
  • Accessible solution for smallholder farmers: Designed around the real problems of smallholder farmers, to give them an accessible tool to support their decisions.

Expected impact

The expected impact is to improve the democratization of access to information for smallholder farmers. We hope this will improve their productivity, which could help level the competitive conditions between small and large producers, thereby supporting the development of local economies.

Tools, programming languages, hardware, and software used

1. Programming languages

  • Python: Used for backend logic, climate analysis, and the agronomic inference engines (requires Python 3.9 or higher).
  • JavaScript and HTML: Make up the frontend user interface and include an integrated agroclimatic and satellite engine in JavaScript to run calculations locally in the browser.
  • Shell scripting: Used in the start.sh script to automate deployment and server startup.

2. Software, frameworks, and libraries

  • Backend: Built on the FastAPI framework and run with the Uvicorn server.
  • Frontend and maps: Single-page application (SPA) using Leaflet.js for map interaction, together with map tiles from OpenStreetMap, CARTO (CartoDB), and Esri World Imagery satellite orthophotos.
  • Environments and dependency management: Python virtual environments (venv) and libraries managed through requirements.txt.

3. APIs, data sources, and hosting

  • NASA APIs and telemetry: Direct integration with the NASA POWER API (historical agrometeorological series), NASA SMAP (surface and root-zone soil moisture), NASA GPM IMERG (accumulated precipitation), the OpenET API (actual evapotranspiration), and NASA HLS / ECOSTRESS (NDVI vegetation vigor and evaporative stress).
  • Other REST APIs: Connection to the ISRIC SoilGrids v2.0 API for soil texture, pH, and organic matter data, and the browser’s W3C Geolocation API.
  • Cloud infrastructure and repository: Source code managed on GitHub, deployed on GitHub Pages for the static frontend and on Render (fieldshift-api.onrender.com) for the backend REST API service.

4. Hardware and instrumentation
The project requires no physical hardware or proprietary sensors installed in the field. Instead, it takes advantage of the satellite network and space instruments of NASA and partner agencies:

  • https://smap.jpl.nasa.gov/data/ → SMAP
  • https://gpm.nasa.gov/data → GPM
  • https://hls.gsfc.nasa.gov/ → HLS
  • https://isric.org/explore/soilgrids → SoilGrids
  • https://etdata.org/api/ → OpenET
  • https://power.larc.nasa.gov/api/pages/ → NASA POWER

Creativity

Our creativity lies in how we integrate existing tools and information in a simple, accessible, and useful way. “We didn’t reinvent the wheel,” as one of our sayings goes. We simply adapted it, in this case, into the bicycle of the smallholder farmer so that they can go further.

What factors did your team consider?

The main factor we considered was the pain points of smallholder farmers. Part of the project’s development involved finding and talking with them, asking for their opinion on what a useful tool would be for them, rather than staying only with complex theory that does not fit local realities.

With that as a starting point, the other factors we took into account were:

Climatological and historical factors

  • agrometeorological series: Analysis of daily climate data (NASA POWER) to establish normal temperatures, interannual rainfall variability, and seasonal patterns.
  • Extreme weather events: Probabilistic calculation of agrometeorological frost and the occurrence of heat waves during the crop window.
  • Agronomic balance laws: Application of principles such as Liebig’s law of the minimum, and adjustments for hemispheric offset depending on the field’s geographic location.

Satellite and hydrological indicators in real time

  • Soil moisture at two depths: Monitoring with NASA SMAP of moisture in the seedbed (0–5 cm) for germination and in the root zone (0–100 cm) for the crop’s available water reserve.
  • Recent water supply and consumption: Measurement of accumulated precipitation over the last 30 days, the SPI-3 drought index, and consumption through actual evapotranspiration.
  • Vegetation vigor and remaining crop residue: Assessment of previous vegetation cover using the NDVI index and the level of foliar evaporative stress, ESI (ECOSTRESS).

Soil properties

  • Soil physics and chemistry: Texture (clay, silt, and sand percentages), water-holding capacity (AWC), organic matter / soil organic carbon (SOC), and soil acidity (pH).
  • Regional calibration: Specific adjustments for local biomes and agricultural zones (such as Córdoba and Santa Fe).

Agronomic history of the field (“Soil Memory”)

  • Predecessor crops and nitrogen fixation: Assessment of the impact of up to 3 previous harvests to measure the replenishment or depletion of residual nitrogen (left by legumes).
  • Biological alternation: Rules for alternating botanical families (for example, grass ↔ legume sequences) and breaking repeated cycles to prevent monoculture and soil degradation.

Crop requirements

  • Catalog of 15 key species: Agronomic calibration based on technical literature and INTA data for cereals, legumes, oilseeds, and specialty crops.
  • Cycle windows and durations: Adjustment of planting dates and the length of the vegetative cycle according to expected water and thermal availability.
